passage:
The principal's room was cold from the air conditioner. Lokesh stood in front of Principal Vidya's desk. His phone was in her drawer, taken because he was said to have used it in class. It was not true, he had only been checking the time for the exam bell.
His first instinct was to say, "This is so unfair, you never listen!" He could feel the words in his mouth. Instead he took a breath. "Ma'am, may I explain? I'd like to say what happened, and then you can decide."
Vidya folded her hands. "Go on."
He told her about the exam clock. She nodded and said, "I'll check with your teacher."

qa.q: Where did Lokesh's phone end up after the incident?
qa.a: Lokesh's phone was in Principal Vidya's drawer.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling as he stood in front of the principal's desk, choosing his words?
qa.a: Lokesh felt indignant and worried about the unfairness. Holding back "this is so unfair" shows he wanted to be heard, not to fight.

qa.q: What did Lokesh choose to say, and what did it change?
qa.a: Lokesh said, "Ma'am, may I explain?" and offered to describe what happened. Vidya folded her hands, listened and promised to check with his teacher.

qa.q: How might Principal Vidya have reacted if Lokesh had said "you never listen"?
qa.a: Vidya would probably have felt challenged and the talk would have turned into a power fight. Instead she listened and agreed to check.

grounding: A teenager who feels unfairly treated speaks to a principal with respectful directness, "may I explain", rather than rudeness.

passage:
"Papa, you said no without even listening!" Uday said, slamming his bag on the sofa.
Gautam looked up from the newspaper. "Watch your tone."
Uday stopped. He looked at the bag, then at his father. "Sorry. That was rude. May I explain why I want to go? Five minutes?"
"Five minutes."
"It's the group project, Papa. Four of us, at Farhan's house, till eight. His mother will be home. I'll text the moment I arrive and the moment I leave."
Gautam folded the paper. "What is the project?"
"Water saving in our colony. We present on Monday."
"Eight sharp, and you call me."
"Deal, Papa. Thank you."

qa.q: Until what time does Uday want to stay at Farhan's house?
qa.a: Uday wants to stay until eight.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he slammed the bag and said Papa had not listened?
qa.a: Uday felt frustrated and dismissed. The slammed bag shows that he was angry at being refused without a hearing.

qa.q: What did Uday change after his father said "Watch your tone", and why did it work?
qa.a: Uday apologised, asked "May I explain?" and gave clear details about who, where and when. That let his father listen and agree with a condition.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been thinking when Uday first shouted?
qa.a: Gautam may have felt disrespected and cautious about the plan. After the apology and details he felt reassured enough to say yes.

grounding: A teenager who argues with a father begins rudely, then uses respectful directness, "may I explain", and is heard.

passage:
The rain had flooded the road, the school bus had broken down, and Omkar ran through the gate forty minutes late, soaked. Mahima Ma'am, the principal, was waiting under the porch with the late register.
"Detention. Saturday."
"That's so unfair! You can't punish me for a bus breaking down!" Omkar's voice rang in the corridor. Two juniors stopped to watch.
Mahima Ma'am's face went still. "Watch your tone."
Omkar felt it: this was about to become a fight he'd lose. He took a breath, wiped the water off his face.
"Sorry, Ma'am. May I explain? Bus number 12 broke down at the flyover. The driver has a note. Six of us are late."
She looked at him for a moment, then at the others coming in behind, all dripping. "Show me the note."
He did. She crossed out his name. "Next time, lead with that."

qa.q: What number was the bus that broke down?
qa.a: Bus number 12 broke down at the flyover.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he shouted that it was unfair?
qa.a: Omkar felt angry and wronged, soaked and punished for something that wasn't his fault.

qa.q: What changed the principal's decision?
qa.a: Omkar calmed down, apologised, asked "May I explain?" and gave clear facts with the driver's note, which respectful directness made easy to accept.

qa.q: How did Mahima Ma'am see Omkar's first outburst?
qa.a: Mahima Ma'am likely saw it as rudeness and a challenge to her authority, which is why she said "Watch your tone."

grounding: A teenager seeking fairness first argues rudely with a principal, then uses respectful directness and is heard.

passage:
In their Kolkata flat, Mehak had been arguing with her mother, Bidisha, for ten minutes. The school fest ended at nine, and Ma wanted her home by seven.
"You treat me like a baby! Everyone else is staying!"
"Mehak, don't raise your voice at me."
"Why not? You never listen anyway!"
Ma turned back to the stove. Mehak could see it: every shout was making the answer more no.
She went to her room and sat for a while. Was she angry about the time, or about winning? A bit of both, honestly.
She came back. "Ma, I'm sorry I shouted. Can I explain my side properly?"
Ma put the spoon down. "Go on."
"I'm on the stage team, so I have to stay until the end. Riya's father is dropping four of us home. I'll text you when I leave."
Ma thought. "Give me Riya's father's number. And text when you reach."

qa.q: When does the school fest end?
qa.a: The school fest ended at nine.

qa.q: What did Mehak realise when she sat in her room?
qa.a: Mehak felt torn, realising she was angry partly about the curfew and partly about wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: Which approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising and asking to explain, then giving clear facts about the stage team and the lift home, worked better because Ma could listen instead of defend.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel during the shouting?
qa.a: Bidisha felt disrespected and closed off, turning back to the stove as Mehak's voice rose.

grounding: A teenager arguing with a parent separates seeking fairness from testing power, and respectful directness works better than rudeness.

passage:
"Vinita, your phone was out during study period. It stays with me till Friday."
"Ma'am, may I explain before you decide?"
Principal Jahnavi Ma'am raised an eyebrow. "Two minutes."
"I wasn't chatting. Our biology teacher asked us to photograph the leaf samples for the project. I have the photos here. I should have asked permission first. That part is my mistake."
"Hm. Show me."
"Here. Twelve photos, all leaves."
"And you didn't ask because?"
"Because Sir said it was fine yesterday, and I assumed it still was. I get why that looks bad."
Ma'am scrolled. "Neha shouted at me about the same thing this morning. Told me I was a dictator."
"I'm not saying you're a dictator, Ma'am. I'm just asking for fairness."
Jahnavi Ma'am handed the phone back. "Next time, a note from Sir. And thank you for talking to me like that."

qa.q: How many photos did Vinita show the principal?
qa.a: Vinita showed twelve photos, all leaves.

qa.q: Why might Vinita have chosen to ask "may I explain"?
qa.a: Vinita was likely anxious but determined, wanting fairness rather than a fight, and hoping to be heard by staying calm.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Vinita calmly explained, showed the evidence and admitted a mistake, which let the principal see Vinita's side fairly.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi Ma'am see Vinita compared with Neha?
qa.a: Jahnavi Ma'am felt respected by Vinita's calm, direct way of speaking, unlike Neha's shouting, and said thank you for it.

grounding: A teenager seeking fairness uses respectful directness with a principal, which works better than a classmate's rudeness.

passage: I'm Ganga, and in Class 9 I learnt the difference between being loud and being heard. The projector in the AV room cracked during lunch, and Tenzin got blamed because he was the last one seen leaving. I was there. I knew he hadn't touched it. So I marched into the principal's office and said, "This is so unfair, you never listen to students!" Principal ma'am's face closed like a door. I got a warning for rudeness, and Tenzin still had to stay after school. That night I was furious. Then I wondered: was I fighting for Tenzin, or fighting to win? Next morning I went back. "Ma'am, may I explain what I saw at lunch?" She put her pen down. I told her about the cable someone had tripped on after Tenzin left. She checked the corridor camera that afternoon, and Tenzin's name came off the list. Same facts. Different door.

qa.q: Where did the projector crack?
qa.a: In the AV room, during lunch.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling that night after the warning?
qa.a: Ganga was furious and also unsure, wondering whether the fight was about fairness for Tenzin or about winning.

qa.q: Which approach worked, and why?
qa.a: "Ma'am, may I explain what I saw?" was direct but respectful, so the principal listened, checked the camera and cleared Tenzin.

qa.q: How might the principal have heard Ganga's first outburst?
qa.a: As an attack on her authority, so she closed off and gave a warning instead of hearing the facts.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose rude outburst to a principal fails while a respectful "may I explain" gets a fair hearing for a classmate.
